\section[o elevador]{o elevador — a lift}

\label{lesson:PT-C88-elevador}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for traffic lights, then the Portuguese for a car park.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o elevador}
\textbf{o elevador} — \textquotedblleft{}a lift\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{elevador} is \textquotedblleft{}a lifter\textquotedblright{}: built from the verb \textquotedblleft{}to raise\textquotedblright{} and \emph{-dor}, \textquotedblleft{}one that does\textquotedblright{}. The verb $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{elevare}, \textquotedblleft{}to lift up\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[o norte]{o norte — the north}

\label{lesson:PT-C88-norte}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for a car park, then the Portuguese for a lift.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o norte}
\textbf{o norte} — \textquotedblleft{}the north\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{norte} $\leftarrow$ French \emph{nord}, \textquotedblleft{}north\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1) — borrowed. The French word came from Old English \emph{norþ}.
\end{cousinweb}

\end{cousinweb}
